case_source: (From the judgment and order dated the 8th and 9th day of December, 1997 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 1377 of 1995).
full_judgment:
Md Fazlul Karim J: The appeal by leave is directed against the judgment and order dated the 8th and 9th day of December, 1997 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 1377 of 1995 discharging the Rule.

2. The appellant filed Case No. 1007 of 1988 before the Chairman, Court of Settlement, Dhaka under Section 7(1) of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985 (Ordinance No. 54 of 1985) stating, inter-alia, that the case property belonged to Rafi Ahmed Fidai who got the same by way of allotment from the then Government of East Pakistan. Rafi Ahmed Fidai sold the suit land to Mrs. Zakia Khatoon at Taka 8,000 on 6-6-1963 and Zakia Khatoon sold the suit property again in favour of the appellant, Mrs. Ambia Khatun for Taka 12,000 by executing a deed of sale on 21-3-1974 and registered the same on 18-4-1974. Zakia Khatoon paid municipal taxes and the appellant which living in the suit property after purchase used to pay electricity bills and WASA bills and the draft RS record in respect of the suit property has been prepared in the name of the appellant and as such, the provisions of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 have no manner of application as the appellant was in possession and no notice was served upon the appellant. So, the inclusion of the case property under Section 5(1)(b) was illegal. The Court of Settlement by its judgment and order dated 20-12-1994 dismissed the case of the appellant for deleting the property from the list of abandoned buildings whereupon the appellant moved the High Court Division against the said judgment and order but the Rule was discharged by the impugned order.

3. Leave was granted to consider that submissions of the learned Counsel for the appellants that—

"the question of 'jurisdictional fact' with regard to non-issuance of statutory notice prior to enlistment of the property in 'Kha' list was specifically raised before the Court of settlement, thereby raising in fact the question of absence of jurisdiction of the Court of settlement over the matter but this question was not considered at all, and without resolving this issue the Court assumed jurisdiction over the matter inasmuch as the respondent Government failed to place any notice even before the High Court Division to justify the jurisdiction of the Court of Settlement over the matter and thus, the High Court Division failed to consider the absence of jurisdiction of the Court of Settlement over the matter. the learned Advocate next submitted that the appellant produced all original title deeds including the deed of sale dated 6-6-1963 executed and registered by the original lessee Rafi Ahmed Fidai in favour of the appellant's vendor Zakia Khatoon, and the said deed was testified to have been recorded by the official of the record room in the relevant volume before the Court of Settlement, but the Court of Settlement having been influenced by extraneous consideration did not consider this vital evidence including the assessment roll for the year 1967-68 and other documents and found erroneously the document of 1963 to be forged and created fraudulently and thus, the High Court Division committed an error of law in discharging the Rule."

4. Mr. MI Farooqui, learned Counsel, appearing for the appellant submitted that the question of 'jurisdictional fact' with regard to non-issuance of statutory notice prior to enlistment of the property in 'Kha' list was specifically raised before the Court of Settlement thereby raising in fact the question of absence of jurisdiction of the Court of Settlement over the matter, but this question was not considered at all and without resolving this issue, the Court of settlement assumed jurisdiction over the matter and the learned Judges of the High Court Division also failed to consider the absence of jurisdiction of the Court of Settlement over the matter inasmuch as the respondent Government failed to place any statutory notice even before the High Court Division to justify the jurisdiction of the Court of Settlement over the matter, and in that view of the matter, the High Court Division committed error of law. The learned Counsel further submitted that appellant produced all original title deeds including original deed of sale dated 06-06-1963 executed and registered by the original lessee Rafi Ahmed Fidai in favour of the appellant's Vendor Zakia Khatoon and the said deed was testified to have been recorded by the official of the record room in the relevant volume before the Court of Settlement but the Court of Settlement having been influenced by extraneous consideration, did not consider this vital evidence on record including the assessment roll for the year 1967-68 and other documents and found erroneously the document of 1963 to be forged and fabricated and the High Court Division also failed to consider this aspect of the case and committed an error of law. The learned Counsel finally submitted that in view of the relevant original title deeds on record and possession lying with the appellant, the 'legitimate inference' would be that the appellant and her vendor had always been in control, management and enjoyment of the property in question, and the finding, contrary by the Court of Settlement, must be held to be an act without jurisdiction, and the High Court Division have committed an error of law by not interfering under Article 102 of the constitution.

5. Mr. MI Farooqui referring to Section 4 of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 argued that it has been stated therein that in pursuance of a notice in any form issued thereunder at any time before 30th October, 1988 the Government may take over possession of any abandoned property or building. This power of issuing this type of notice in any form gave arbitrary power to the Government and hence is void ability, He further referring to Section 4 (b) (ii) of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 and contends that no building shall be taken possession of as abandoned property under President Order No. 16 of 1972 except in pursuance of a notice in any from issued under PO No. 16 of 1972 and no such notice is issued in respect of a building, in execution of a decree or order passed by a Court in a suit filed by the Government. He submitted that this is clear discrimination in equality and is hit by equality clause under Article 27 and 31 of the Constitution.

6. Mr. MK Rahman, learned Additional Attorney-General appearing for the respondents submitted that the document in favour of Zakia Khatoon alleged to have been executed by Rafi Ahamed Fidai on 6-6-1963 were forged, null and void and mere paper transaction and has been created by false personation inasmuch as the signature of Rafi Ahmed Fidai appearing on his deed does not tally with the signature of Rafi Ahmed Fidai in the alleged sale deed. The sale deed alleged to have been executed by Zakia Khatoon in favour of the petitioner on 21-3-1974 is also void, inoperative, without consideration and a paper transaction and the same is hit by Article 6 of PO No. 16 of 1972. Furthermore, the LTI is quite different from the alleged LTI of Zakia Khatoon inasmuch as said Zakia Khatoon had no existence and her name was never mutated with the Housing and Settlement Department. It was found by the Court of Settlement on consideration of the alleged transfer deed and evidence on record that Rafi Ahmed Fidai never transferred the property to Zakia Khatoon or anybody else. Rafi Ahmed Fidai was a non-local and during liberation war his whereabouts were not known and he ceased to manage, occupy and supervise the case property in person, hence the property was rightly vested in the Government as abandoned under PO No. 16 of 1972; that Zakia Khatoon, the vendor of the writ petitioner was a fake person who did not purchase the land from original owner Rafi Ahmed Fidai. Zakia Khatoon was not examined in this case before the Court of Settlement and no evidence came before the Court about the existence of alleged Zakia Khatoon inasmuch as her signature in the first page of the kabala executed in favour of Ambia Khatun does not tally with LTI in the rest of the pages of the deed and the expert opined in the similar way. The Court of settlement also came to a finding about the fakeness of Zakia Khatoon and that she was a fictitious person. So, the question of purchase of the case property by Zakia Khatoon on 6th June, 1963 does not at all arise. Accordingly, the purchase of the case property by the present writ petitioner from her does not arise. Her Kabala and the kabala in the name of Zakia are products of false personation. All these are findings of facts in a petition, so the High Court Division cannot look into it. The findings of the Court of Settlement are based on facts and materials produced before it. The High Court Division could interfere with the findings of facts under its jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution only if it could be shown that the tribunal had acted without jurisdiction or made any finding upon no evidence or without considering any materials evidence and facts causing prejudice to the complaining party or that it had acted malafide or in violation of any principle or natural justice.

7. The learned Additional Attorney-General, appearing for the respondents further submitted that Article 25 of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 clearly provides that the Government may make rules for carrying out the purposes of the order and in exercise of such power Government has framed the notice in the form in exercise of the power vested under Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Taking over Possession) Rules, 1972 and in rule 6 residential and other buildings in the urban area have been classified as one category of abandoned property. For taking over possession of abandoned property, notice in Form I, II, III and IV as the case may be issued. The learned Counsel urged that notice in any form means depending on the category of abandoned property and notice in any form of the specimen given as per rule 3 should be issued before taking over of the abandoned property. So, there is no violation of any law and it was not arbitrary. Mr. Rahman submitted that the Appellate Division held that once the property is listed as abandoned property it must be presumed that Government has formed opinion regarding abandoned character of the property as defined in Article 2 of the PO No. 16 of 1972.

8. The learned Counsel for the appellant though strenuously argued regarding the jurisdiction issue of the Court having no initial jurisdiction in the matter to enquire into the question regarding the assumption of jurisdiction on the plea of absence of any notice require under the Abandoned Property Order, 1972 has lost sight of the fact that the property automatically vested as Abandoned Property upon commencement of the said order inasmuch as the impugned notice dated 17-3-1986 was not a notice treating the property as abandoned one. Accordingly the question of 'jurisdictional fact' regarding non-issuance of statutory notice prior to enlistment of the property as abandoned property was of no substance.

9. Mr. MI Farooqui, learned Counsel, has cited a decision in support of the above contention in the case of Baldwin and Francis Ltd as Parents Appeal Tribunal reported in (1959) AC 663 which arose to consider the effect of Sections 9(3), 14(4), 85 and 87 of the Patents Act, 1949, that no appeal lay to the Court of Appeal from the decision of the Parents Appeal Tribunal in the said proceedings, that it was an inferior tribunal and that the only remedy of persons aggrieved by its decision was by way of an order of certiorari.

10. The fact leading to the case that was a company made an application for a patent, whereupon, on the publication of its specification, the owners of a prior dated patent holder opposed the application on the ground, inter-alia, that its specification could not fairly describe the invention or method by which it was to be performed without referring to their prior dated patent, and that such a reference should be directed under Section 9 of the Act. Both the patents applied for and the prior dated patent concerned improvements designed to prevent the re-closing of an electric circuit in which an earth fault had developed, until that fault was repaired. In opposition proceedings under Section 14, the superintending examiner, on behalf of the comptroller, decided that the later invention could not be performed without substantial risk of infringement of the prior dated patent, and, accordingly, there being no proposals for amending its specification, the superintending examiner, by a final decision, ordered that the patent applied for should be sealed with a reference to the prior dated patent. On appeal, the Patents Appeal Tribunal reversed this decision. The owners of the prior dated patent applied for an order of certiorari on the ground that there was error of law appearing on the face of the record in that the tribunal had misconstrued the rival specifications or one of them.

11. In the said decision it was held, inter alia, that—

"In some of those cases it has been said that the tribunal, in falling into an error of this particular kind, has exceeded its jurisdiction. No tribunal, it is said, has any jurisdiction to be influenced by extraneous considerations or to disregard vital matters. This is good sense and enables the Court of Queen's Bench to receive evidence to prove the error. But an excess of jurisdiction in this sense is very different from want of jurisdiction altogether which is, of course, determinable at the commencement, not at the conclusion of the inquiry, whereas an excess of jurisdiction is determinable in the course of or at the end of inquiry. But allowing that a tribunal which falls into an error of this particular kind does exceed its jurisdiction, as I am prepared to do, nevertheless I am quite clear that at the same time it falls into an error of law too; for the simple reason that it has not determined according to law.' That it indeed, how Blackburn J put it in Reg vs De Reuzen And the decision in the Northumberland case itself shows that, even though no evidence is given, nevertheless if such an error appears from the documents properly before the Court, or by legitimate inference therefrom, then certiorari may be granted to quash the decision; and the certiorari can properly be said to be for error of law on the face of the proceedings. It may be excess of jurisdiction as well, but it is certainly error of law."

12. The cited decision has also no application in the facts and circumstances of the instant case because the starting point of possession and alleged ownership of Zakia was on and from 18-04-1974 when the property has already vested as an abandoned property by operation of Section 4 of the Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposed of) Order, 1972, PO No. 16 of 1972 effective from 28-2-1972. Thus, it is too late in the day to allege they want of jurisdiction of the Tribunal to allege that there was no notice treating the property as an abandoned one when the property has already vested before the alleged pure phase on 18-4-1974 by the writ-petitioner and ignoring the very fact that the writ-petitioner herself resorted to the jurisdiction of the Court of Settlement challenging the alleged notice dated 17-3-1986 in order to raise the question of issuance to jurisdictional fact or want of jurisdiction before the High Court Division in writ jurisdiction, although the same is not at all relevant in the matter inasmuch as there is no error occurring was alleged effecting the alleged jurisdiction and accordingly there is no such illegality for assuming jurisdiction in certiorari as there is also no error of law on the face of the proceeding. It is to be borne in mind that the writ petitioner herself filed the case before the Tribunal thereby surrendering to the jurisdiction of the Tribunal. In any view of the matter on the given fact the writ petition is not maintainable challenging treating of the property as an abandoned one.

13. Section 2(1) of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property Order, 1972 defined Abandoned Property as under:

(1) "abandoned property" means any property owned by any person who is not present in Bangladesh or whose whereabouts are not known or who has ceased to occupy supervise or manage in person his property, including—

Inclusion clauses

(i) any property owned by any person who is a citizen of a State which at any time after the 25th day of March, 1971, was at war with or engaged in military operation against the People's Republic of Bangladesh;

(ii) any property taken over under the Bangladesh (Taking over of Control and Management of Industrial and Commercial Concerns) Order, 1972(Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972), but does not include-

Exclusion clauses

(a) any property the owner of which is residing outside Bangladesh for any purpose which, in the opinion of the Government, is not prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh;

(b) any property which is in the possession or under the control of the Government under any law for the time being in force.

Explanation —"Person who is not present in Bangladesh" includes anybody of persons or company constituted or incorporated in the territory or under the laws of a State which at any time after the 25th day of March, 1971, was at war with or engaged in military operations against the People's Republic of Bangladesh.

14. Article 4 thereof provides that "On commencement of this Order, all abandoned properties in Bangladesh shall vest in the Government and shall be administered, controlled, managed and disposed of, by the transfer or otherwise, in accordance with the provisions of this Order.

15. Thus, since the whereabouts or otherwise of the original allotted Rafi Ahmed Fidai was not known or that there was nobody found to control, manage or otherwise, the property became an abandoned property by operation of law.

16. The appellant was alleged to have been inducted in the building pursuant to the sale deed dated 18-4-1974 although the said property became abandoned property pursuant to the provision of PO No. 16 of 1972 on and from 28th February, 1972 and vested in the Government as under Article 4 the vesting was automatic. Moreover, the appellant did not allege any instances of illegality or irregularity either of law and on fact regarding the abandoned character of the property prior to her alleged purchase on 18-4-1974 but has simply impugned the issuance of alleged or notice contained in Memo No. 9/619 dated 17-3-1986 in favour of Ambia Khatoon stating that;

"এই বাড়ীতে বসবাসের স্বপক্ষে আপনার নিকট যে কাগজপত্র আছে তাহা আগামী ১০(দশ) দিনের মধ্যে এই অফিসে দেখাইবার জন্য অনুরোধ করা যাইতেছে। উল্লেখ্য যে, বাড়ীটি অত্র মন্ত্রণালয়ের পরিত্যক্ত তালিকায় অর্ন্তগত আছে বলিয়া দেখা যায়। সরকারী এই কাজে আপনার সহযোগিতা আমাদের কাম্য। "

17. From the aforesaid impugned notice in the writ petition it is apparent that it has simply asked the alleged occupant to produce any paper in support of her alleged possession within 10 days from the date stating further that the house in question has already been enlisted in the list of abandoned property. So apparently the said property has already been vested in the Government and treated as abandoned property and the purport of the notice, as it appears, was only to ascertain the alleged nature possession of the said Mosammat Ambia Khatoon in the abandoned property and to show the basis for such possession in the house which is an abandoned property.

18. In that view of the matter no question of any alleged jurisdictional fact with regard to the non-issuance of any statutory notice prior to the declaration of the building as abandoned one or enlistment of the property in 'K' list under the provision of supplementary provision of 1985 was involved. Moreso, the present alleged occupant, Ambia Khatoon was allegedly inducted in the property only on 18-4-1974 upon her alleged purchase of the date and as such, the question of absence of jurisdiction of the Court of Settlement in the matter on the alleged issuance of impugned notice giving rise to jurisdictional fat do not arise and hence the ultimate resolution of the issue before the Settlement Court regarding ascertainment of the alleged possession of Ambia Khatoon by the Court of Settlement was with jurisdiction.

19. It appears that the original allotment of the building from Housing and Settlement Department was in favour of Rafi Ahmed Fidai, the admitted original lessee pursuant to a deed of lease dated 1-1-1960 but the alleged transfer either in favour of Zakia Khatoon on 6-6-1963 or in favour of Ambia Khatoon on 18-4-1974 was neither through a legal document i.e. a deed of lease of deed of sale with no intimation whatsoever to the Housing and Settlement Department as to the transfer by the alleged deeds and that Ambia Khatoon has also failed to produce Zakia before the authority or Court of Settlement and the alleged identity of said Zakia Khatoon has not been proved. Furthermore, the alleged deeds of Zakia Khatoon and Ambia Khatoon dated 18-4-1974 were found to be forged by the Court of Settlement.

20. Be it mentioned here that Ambia Khatoon filed the Case No. 1007 of 1998 for alleged release of the instant house No. 8/15, block-D, Salimullah Road, Mohammadpur, Dhaka and the Court of Settlement on perusal of the materials on record and the deposition of the parties found that the alleged transfer from original allottee, Rafi Ahmed Fidai in favour of alleged Zakia Khatoon is not backed by the evidence on record. Exhibit 5 is Form 'A' showing application for certificate under Section 3 of the Transfer of Properties (Pakistan) Ordinance, 1947. This Exhibit 5 dated 15-5-1963. Its serial No. 9 shows consideration for which the property is intended to transfer. In this serial no Rs 9000 only is written. If it was intended to sell at Rs. 9000 the sale deed would have contained the same consideration. On enquiry of the sale deed in favour of Zakia Khatoon by Rafi Ahmed Fidai shows that Rafi Ahmed Fidai allegedly sold the case property at Taka 8,000. Thus, either kabala is false or the said Form 'A' is false.

21. The Court of Settlement further proceeded to hold that PW 1 Rahman Jahangir produced papers relating to payment of taxes to Dhaka Municipality in Exhibit 12 series; this document do not relate to the case property of 8/15 Salimullah Road, Mohammadpur, Dhaka. Instead it relates to 105 of Quaid-e-Azam Road. Moreover, one Zakia Khatoon is related to a property in 8/15 Razia Sultana Road but the case property is of 8/15, block-D, Salimullah Road. The Court of Settlement upon considering the relevant material on record has doubted about the existence of any woman named Zakir Khatoon from whom the appellant allegedly purchased on 21-3-1974. The Court of Settlement also held that no voter's list or any of this sort was produced to show that Zakia Khatoon was a voter at the elections including that on Paurashava election and has held that the appellant's alleged purchase was a fake purchase and the reason being fake purchase based on some forged and invalid document also for the reason that Rafi Ahmed Fidai got the allotment for the house at Taka 3000 in the year of 1960 and the alleged purchase in favour of Zakia Khatoon in the year, 1963 was for Taka 8000 within the lapse of 3 years. But the alleged purchase in favour of Ambia Khatoon on 1974 was only for 12,000 for the house which was abnormally low price. The Tribunal also held that the alleged transfer by the alleged Zakia Khatoon in favour of Ambia Khatoon was on the basis of a false and fake document as the appellant could not produce Zakia Khatoon in the Court and that her alleged LTI in first page of kabala in favour of Ambia Khatoon does not tally with LTI in rest of the pages of the document which was affirmed by the report of the expert. It is in evidence of PW1 Noor Jahan Begum, wife of Rafi Ahmed Fidai, the original allotte that it found one Rahman Jahangir, PW 1 as the occupant of the house just after independence of Bangladesh and who as well could not recognize Zakia Khatoon or Ambia Khatoon. So, admittedly one Rahman Jahangir PW 1 was in illegal possession of the case property on 28-2-1972 in absence of Rafi Ahmed Fidai, the original allotted and considering all the aspects of the case the Tribunal held that Zakia Khatoon was fictitious a person and that the alleged transfer by Rafi Ahmed Fidai in favour of Zakia Khatoon was denied by his wife, Noor Jahan Begum and that the alleged kabalas are the products of false personation. As regard the possession of the document and papers by Ambia Khatoon PW 1 Noor Jahan Begum deposed that after liberation her articles and papers were stolen from her case house has substance and that taking the advantage of the possession of the said papers of the same house Ambia Khatoon has raised the plea of purchase by way of a forged document obtained through false personation and accordingly the Tribunal as well found that the appellant. Ambia Khatoon an impostor through improper means at least by means as stated by PW 1 Noor Jahan Begum, the wife of original lessee, Rafi Ahmed Fidai and accordingly the Tribunal held that "since the appellant Ambia Khatoon in Case No. 1007 of 1998 has not furnished facts about possession of the case property on or before commencement of PO No. 16 of 1972 and since we have held that entire transaction of sale as false and fake the case property as absolutely abandoned property," and accordingly held that from the evidence Noor Jahan Begum the admitted wife of Rafi Ahmed Fidai and on her son of Safi Ahmed Fidai that the property was abandoned by them during the liberation war in 1971 and it has been rightly held to be abandoned property within the meaning of Section 2(1) of the PO No. 16 of 1972 and accordingly vested in the Government. The Tribunal has further held that the sale deed in the name of Zakia Khatoon and Ambia Khatoon having been forged and fabricated such deeds do not confer any title and ownership in the case property inasmuch as under Article 6 of PO No. 16 of 1972 such sale is null and void. The Tribunal has held that the inclusion of the case property in the 'Kha' list of the abandoned building was rightly done and thus held that there is no scope for exclusion of the case property from such list.

22. As against the said finding of Court of Settlement the High Court Division as well observed that the findings of the fact arrived at by the Tribunal cannot be looked into in this petition or in writ certiorari as because the finding of the Court of Settlement are based on facts and materials produced before it and the Court is not to interfere with the said findings of facts under its jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution. The Tribunal in its view, has not acted without jurisdiction or made any finding without any basis or without considering any material evidence and facts cause prejudice to the writ-petitioner or that it has acted malafide or in violation of principle of natural justice.

23. In the case of Mostafa Kamal vs. First Court of Settlement reported in 48 DLR (AD) 61 wherein it has been held that;

"Court of Settlement on consideration of materials on record arrived at a finding that Nasima Khatun is not the daughter and heir of original lessee Mohina Khatun and that the said lessee has not been in possession of the house in question at the relevant time. The learned Judges of the High Court Division upon taking into consideration of such clear finding of facts of the Court of settlement refused rightly to interfere with the judgment of that Court upon a correct appreciation of the legal principle that the High Court Division in exercise of its writ jurisdiction cannot sit as a Court of Appeal over the judgment of the Court of Settlement for resetting questions of fact. Thus, we find no illegality in the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division."

24. In the case of Government of Bangladesh vs. Md Jalil reported in 48 DLR (AD) 10 = 15 BLD (AD) 175 = 49 DLR (AD) 26 wherein it has been held that;

"It must be said that the High Court Division failed to appreciate the purport of the judgment of the Court of Settlement as a whole. The Court of Settlement not only disbelieved the testimony as to the alleged death of Alimannessa and burial in Mohammadpur on 10-3-1975, but also disbelieved that evidence adduced by the respondents in its entirety, the inconsistencies in the evidence as to their possession of the disputed house till June 1974 were pointed out and it was observed that by resorting to tricks to falsely prove their mother's death on 10-3-1975 in Bangladesh they not only be-fooled themselves but also exhibited a conduct which compelled the Court "to take an adverse view against the petitioners case". It was clearly found that the respondents failed to disprove the stand taken by the Government that Alimannessa was not present in Bangladesh on 28-2-1972 which means that their evidence as to alleged possession of the disputed house till June 1974 was also disbelieved. That being the position the High Court Division was not at all justified in holding that the Court of settlement filed to taken notice of the evidence of the respondents as to their possession of the disputed house. The High Court Division having no other reason did not at all act legally and property in interfering with the findings of fact made by the Court of Settlement. The High Court Division was not a Court of Appeal required to make determination of facts on its own. It could interfere with the findings of a tribunal of fact under its extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 102 only if it could be shown that the tribunal had acted without jurisdiction or made any finding upon no evidence or without considering any material evidence and facts causing prejudice to the complaining party or that it has acted malafide or in violation of any principle of natural justice. In the absence of any of these conditions the interference by the High Court Division will itself be an act of without jurisdiction. This precisely has happened in the present case and therefore, this appeal must succeed."

<u>25. It appears that admittedly the property has been listed as an abandoned property. Thus, the onus lies upon the appellant to rebut the presumption provided in subsection (2) of Section 5 that the same was not an abandoned property No oral evidence has been adduced before the settlement Court of prove that on 28-2-1972 when President's Order No. 16 of 1972 was promulgated the original lessee, Rafi Ahmed Fidai had been present in Bangladesh or his whereabouts were known or that he did not cease to occupy, supervise or manage in person the house in question and the said position was admitted by PW 1 Nurjahan Begum, the wife of Rafi Ahmed Fidai. The Court of Settlement upon assigning cogent reasons held that the kabala of the appellant's vendor is forged and fabricated document and the original lessee, Rafi Ahmed Fidai did never appear physically before any authority for any purpose after the liberation war in Bangladesh. The High Court Division has thus, rightly, maintained the order of the Court of Settlement by the impugned judgment and order. It also appears that the High Court Division upon examining the different provisions of the Ordinance of 1985 including section 7 came to the finding that the said section can give the appellant exactly the same remedy which she was praying for in the petition, that the Court of Settlement has been given the specific power to exclude the disputed property from the impugned list. The appellant has urged before the Court of Settlement that the building is not an abandoned property or that it has not vested in the Government and that her right or interest in the building has not been affected by the provisions of PO No. 16 of 1972. But in the facts and circumstances of the case when the State has devised an alternative forum for giving complete relief to the appellant, the learned Judges observed, she could not invoke the writ jurisdiction without exhausting the remedy provided for in the Ordinance.</u>

<u>26. In the instant case the broad fact alleged by the writ-petitioner, Ambia Khatoon is that she is the transferee from one Zakia Khatoon vide a deed of sale executed and registered on 18-4-1974. Zakir Khatoon allegedly purchased the property from the original allottee, Rafi Ahmed Fidai executed on 6-6-1963 in her favour and the said deed of Zakia Khatoon has highly been disputed and the same was neither produced in the case nor any material was placed before the Court to substantiate the sale of Rafi Ahmed Fidai in favour of Zakia Khatoon so as to devolve the interest of Zakia Khatoon in favour of the writ-petitioner Ambia Khatoon pursuant to her alleged purchase dated 18-4-1974.</u>

<u>27. Be that as it may, we are concerned with the property which has been vested as abandoned property pursuant to the PO No. 16 of 1972 as admittedly neither Rafi Ahmed Fidai nor the alleged Zakia Khatoon could be found in possession or control to manage the property on 28-2-1972 when the PO No. 16 of 1972 came of effective.</u>

28. In view of the above, we find no substance in the submissions of the learned Counsel for the appellant.

29. Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs.

End.
